newsitem.title: USA: U.S. on track to put Elk Hills reserve up for sale.
newsitem.headline: U.S. on track to put Elk Hills reserve up for sale.

text.p: The U.S. Energy Department is on track to put its share of the Elk Hills oil and gas field in California up for sale in April, a senior Energy Department official said Wednesday.

"The Department remains on schedule to place the government's portion of the Elk Hills field on the market and determine if its market value exceeds the value of the field under continued government ownership," assistant energy secretary Patricia Fry Godley said in testimony to a House Science Committee panel.

The privatization of Elk Hills, which last year produced about 60,000 barrels per day of oil and about 358 million cubic feet per day of natural gas, is expected to be one of the largest federal asset sales ever.
"We're very pleased with the interest expressed so far," a fossil energy official said. "We think we're going to have a wide competition."
Although the department expects to put its majority stake up for bids next month, it has yet to determine exactly what will be up for sale.
"It still is planned for April," the fossil energy official said. "The key point yet to be made public is the actual percentage shares we would offer."
Under the law calling for privatization of Elk Hills, the government was supposed to finalize its equity stake in each section of the field last October. That deadline has now been moved to May 10.
"Bids on shares can be adjusted up or down once equity is determined," the fossil energy aide said.
The department plans to offer its share in pieces, with an operator interest and several nonworking interests.
Elk Hills co-owner Chevron USA Production Co says assessments on equity stakes in three out of four sections of the field have been completed.

For the Dry Gas Zone, an independent assessor recommended raising the government's stake to 84 percent from 77 percent. For Carneros, the recommendation was to reduce the government's stake to 97 percent from 100 percent.
For the Shallow Oil Zone the assessor recommended reducing the government's stake to 66 percent from 70 percent.
A dispute continues over the largest zone, Stevens, according to Mike Stay, Chevron's Elk Hills program director.
The Energy Department expects to select the best bids in the fall and complete a sale if it gets the right price by February 10, 1998.
